DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION: The Limits of Constitutional Freedom

Directions: Read all three documents below carefully. Then respond to the prompt using evidence from all three documents and your knowledge of U.S. history. Apply the HIPP (Historical Context, Intended Audience, Purpose, Point of View) framework to evaluate at least two of the three documents.

---

DOCUMENT A
Source: 13th Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified December 6, 1865. National Archives, Record Group 11.

"Section 1. Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction.
Section 2. Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation."

---

DOCUMENT B
Source: Mississippi Black Code — An Act to Confer Civil Rights on Freedmen, and for Other Purposes, November 25, 1865. Mississippi Laws, Session of 1865, pp. 82–90. (Public domain, pre-1928 state statute.)

"That all freedmen, free negroes, and mulattoes may sue and be sued, implead and be impleaded, in all the courts of law and equity of this State, and may acquire personal property, and choses in action, by descent or purchase, and may dispose of the same in the same manner and to the same extent that white persons may: Provided, That the provisions of this section shall not be so construed as to allow any freedman, free negro, or mulatto to rent or lease any lands or tenements except in incorporated cities or towns, in which places the corporate authorities shall control the same... Every civil officer shall, and every person may, arrest and carry back to his or her legal employer any freedman, free negro, or mulatto who shall have quit the service of his or her employer before the expiration of his or her term of service without good cause."

---

DOCUMENT C
Source: Frederick Douglass, 'The Need for Continuing Anti-Slavery Work,' speech delivered at the 32nd Annual Meeting of the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society, Boston, January 26, 1865. Published in The Liberator, February 10, 1865. (Public domain.)

"I know that many are impatient at the thought of continuing this [anti-slavery] movement now that slavery is abolished. They say it is all over. The work is done. ... But I take a different view. The abolition of slavery is not the abolition of caste. The abolition of slavery is not the abolition of all the disabilities under which the colored people labored. The work of the Anti-Slavery Society will not be done until the colored man is admitted a full member in good and regular standing in the American body politic."

---

PROMPT: Using all three documents and your knowledge of U.S. history, write a well-developed response that addresses the following:

1. Analyze what the 13th Amendment (Document A) did and did not accomplish for Black Americans in 1865. How does its exception clause create a structural vulnerability that Documents B and C illuminate?
2. Apply HIPP analysis to at least TWO of the three documents: identify the Historical Context, Intended Audience, Purpose, and Point of View of each, and explain how these factors shape the meaning and limitations of each document as evidence.
3. Using all three documents and your historical knowledge, construct a historical argument that answers: Did the abolition of slavery in 1865 constitute genuine freedom? Support your argument with specific evidence from the documents and relevant knowledge about the Freedmen's Bureau (US.04), the 14th Amendment (US.02), and the political context of Reconstruction (US.05).
4. Explain what Document C (Douglass, January 1865) predicts — and evaluate the accuracy of his prediction based on the evidence of Document B (Mississippi Black Codes, November 1865).
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS: Los Límites de la Libertad Constitucional

Instrucciones: Lea los tres documentos a continuación con cuidado. Luego responda al indicador usando evidencia de los tres documentos y su conocimiento de la historia de EE.UU. Aplique el marco HIPP (Contexto Histórico, Audiencia Prevista, Propósito, Punto de Vista) para evaluar al menos dos de los tres documentos.

---

DOCUMENTO A
Fuente: 13.ª Enmienda a la Constitución de los Estados Unidos, ratificada el 6 de diciembre de 1865. Archivos Nacionales, Grupo de Registros 11.

«Sección 1. Ni la esclavitud ni la servidumbre involuntaria, excepto como castigo por un delito del que la parte haya sido debidamente condenada, existirán en los Estados Unidos ni en ningún lugar sujeto a su jurisdicción.
Sección 2. El Congreso tendrá poder para hacer cumplir este artículo mediante legislación apropiada.»

---

DOCUMENTO B
Fuente: Código Negro de Mississippi — Ley para Conferir Derechos Civiles a los Libertos y para Otros Fines, 25 de noviembre de 1865. Leyes de Mississippi, Sesión de 1865, pp. 82–90.

«Que todos los libertos, negros libres y mulatos podrán demandar y ser demandados... y podrán adquirir bienes personales... Siempre que las disposiciones de esta sección no se interpreten de modo que permitan a ningún liberto, negro libre o mulato arrendar o alquilar tierras o viviendas excepto en ciudades o pueblos incorporados... Todo funcionario civil deberá, y cualquier persona puede, arrestar y devolver a su empleador legal a cualquier liberto, negro libre o mulato que haya abandonado el servicio de su empleador antes de la expiración de su período de servicio sin buena causa.»

---

DOCUMENTO C
Fuente: Frederick Douglass, 'La Necesidad de Continuar el Trabajo Antiesclavista', discurso pronunciado en la 32.ª Reunión Anual de la Sociedad Abolicionista de Massachusetts, Boston, 26 de enero de 1865. Publicado en The Liberator, 10 de febrero de 1865. (Dominio público.)

«Sé que muchos están impacientes ante la idea de continuar este movimiento [antiesclavista] ahora que la esclavitud ha sido abolida. Dicen que ya terminó. El trabajo está hecho. ... Pero tengo una visión diferente. La abolición de la esclavitud no es la abolición de la casta. La abolición de la esclavitud no es la abolición de todas las discapacidades bajo las cuales laboraba la gente de color. El trabajo de la Sociedad Antiesclavista no estará hecho hasta que el hombre de color sea admitido como miembro de pleno derecho en la buena y regular situación del cuerpo político americano.»

---

INDICADOR: Usando los tres documentos y su conocimiento de la historia de EE.UU., escriba una respuesta bien desarrollada que aborde lo siguiente:
1. Analice lo que la 13.ª Enmienda (Documento A) logró y no logró para los afroamericanos en 1865.
2. Aplique el análisis HIPP a al menos DOS de los tres documentos.
3. Construya un argumento histórico que responda: ¿Constituyó la abolición de la esclavitud en 1865 una libertad genuina?
4. Explique lo que predice el Documento C (Douglass, enero de 1865) y evalúe la precisión de su predicción basándose en la evidencia del Documento B.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response (6/6) will include: (1) Precise analysis of the 13th Amendment's accomplishment (abolition of chattel slavery) and its structural gap (the punishment-for-crime exception, plus the absence of citizenship or equal protection guarantees). (2) Full HIPP analysis of at least two documents — e.g., Document A: Historical context = immediate post-Civil War, ratified before any Reconstruction framework was in place; Intended audience = the nation and the states; Purpose = to constitutionalize the Emancipation Proclamation and permanently end slavery; Point of View = reflects federal power but does not address social or economic conditions of freedom. Document B: Historical context = within weeks of the 13th Amendment's ratification, Southern states moved to re-impose control; Intended audience = white Mississippians seeking to maintain labor control and racial hierarchy; Purpose = to define the status and restrictions on freedpeople in ways that restore economic dependency; Point of View = reflects planter-class perspective that the social order of racial hierarchy must be preserved under new legal forms. (3) Historical argument: Abolition in 1865 constituted a legal end to chattel slavery but not genuine freedom — genuine freedom requires civil rights (equal protection, citizenship: 14th Amendment), political rights (15th Amendment), material resources (Freedmen's Bureau land redistribution, which failed), and social equality that the Black Codes systematically denied. (4) Douglass's January 1865 prediction — 'abolition of slavery is not the abolition of caste' — is precisely confirmed by Document B, which shows that Mississippi moved immediately to maintain racial caste through law within weeks of the 13th Amendment's ratification.

items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):

6 - Exemplary: Responds to all four parts of the prompt with historical accuracy and analytical depth. HIPP analysis of two documents is complete and accurate — all four elements addressed for each document, with explanation of how each element shapes the document's meaning as evidence. Historical argument in Part 3 is explicitly organized around a defensible thesis with specific evidence from all three documents AND accurate knowledge of Freedmen's Bureau, 14th Amendment, and Reconstruction context. Cross-document synthesis is explicit — student uses documents against each other and identifies convergent and divergent perspectives. Douglass prediction analysis (Part 4) directly quotes or closely paraphrases both documents and evaluates accuracy with specific evidence.

5 - Advanced: Responds to all four parts with accuracy. HIPP analysis of two documents is mostly complete — may be incomplete on one element for one document. Historical argument is thesis-driven with evidence from all three documents and one or two of the named historical contexts (Freedmen's Bureau, 14th Amendment, Reconstruction). Cross-document synthesis is present. Douglass prediction analysis is accurate and specific.

4 - Proficient: Responds to all four parts with basic accuracy. HIPP analysis is present for two documents but incomplete — one or two elements missing or underdeveloped per document. Historical argument addresses the core question with evidence from at least two documents. Douglass prediction analysis is present but may be general.

3 - Adequate: Responds to most parts (3 of 4) with basic accuracy. HIPP analysis is attempted for at least one document but incomplete. Historical argument is present but may describe rather than argue. Evidence primarily from one or two documents.

2 - Developing: Responds to one or two parts. HIPP analysis is attempted but mostly incorrect or confused. Historical argument is asserted without evidence. May accurately summarize documents without synthesizing them.

1 - Beginning: Some accurate historical content present but no analytical structure. Student may describe one document without HIPP analysis or cross-document synthesis.

0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS:
- Document A HIPP: Historical context (end of Civil War, no Reconstruction framework yet); Audience (national, constitutional); Purpose (permanent abolition); Point of View (federal legal perspective, silent on social conditions) — plus the significance of the exception clause.
- Document B HIPP: Historical context (Southern states' immediate resistance to emancipation's implications); Audience (white Mississippians, state legislature); Purpose (re-establish racial labor control under legal form); Point of View (planter-class, white supremacist social order).
- Document C HIPP: Historical context (January 1865 — before ratification, before war's end); Audience (Massachusetts abolitionists — sympathetic); Purpose (sustain momentum, prevent premature dissolution of anti-slavery movement); Point of View (Black abolitionist, lived experience of racial oppression beyond legal slavery).

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: 13th Amendment exception clause; Mississippi labor/vagrancy/apprenticeship laws; Douglass's 'abolition of caste' framing; Freedmen's Bureau land redistribution failure (Johnson's amnesty proclamations restoring Confederate property); 14th Amendment (1868) as response to inadequacy of 13th; Black Codes as model for Jim Crow laws later; political compromise between moderate and radical Republicans.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):

6 - Ejemplar: Responde a las cuatro partes del indicador con precisión histórica y profundidad analítica. El análisis HIPP de dos documentos es completo y preciso — los cuatro elementos abordados para cada documento, con explicación de cómo cada elemento moldea el significado del documento como evidencia. El argumento histórico en la Parte 3 está explícitamente organizado alrededor de una tesis defendible con evidencia específica de los tres documentos Y conocimiento preciso del contexto de la Oficina de Libertos, la 14.ª Enmienda y la Reconstrucción.

5 - Avanzado: Responde a las cuatro partes con precisión. El análisis HIPP de dos documentos es mayormente completo. El argumento histórico está impulsado por una tesis con evidencia de los tres documentos y uno o dos de los contextos históricos nombrados.

4 - Competente: Responde a las cuatro partes con precisión básica. El análisis HIPP está presente para dos documentos pero incompleto. El argumento histórico aborda la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos documentos.

3 - Adecuado: Responde a la mayoría de las partes (3 de 4) con precisión básica. El análisis HIPP se intenta para al menos un documento pero está incompleto.

2 - En desarrollo: Responde a una o dos partes. El análisis HIPP se intenta pero es mayormente incorrecto. El argumento histórico es afirmado sin evidencia.

1 - Inicial: Contenido histórico preciso pero sin estructura analítica.

0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EXPECTATIVAS DE ANÁLISIS DOCUMENTAL: HIPP completo para Documentos A, B y C como se describe en inglés. EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Cláusula de excepción de la 13.ª Enmienda; leyes de trabajo/vagabundaje/aprendizaje de Mississippi; marco de 'abolición de la casta' de Douglass; fracaso de la redistribución de tierras de la Oficina de Libertos; 14.ª Enmienda como respuesta a la insuficiencia de la 13.ª; los Códigos Negros como modelo para las leyes de Jim Crow.

items.stem:
DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION: The Compromise of 1877 and the End of Reconstruction

Directions: Read all three documents carefully. Then respond to the prompt using evidence from all three documents and your knowledge of U.S. history. Apply the HIPP (Historical Context, Intended Audience, Purpose, Point of View) framework to evaluate at least two of the three documents.

---

DOCUMENT A
Source: Excerpt from the Report of the Electoral Commission established by Congress to resolve the disputed 1881 presidential election, February 1877. Congressional Record, 44th Congress, 2nd Session. (Public domain, government document.)

"In the matter of the electoral votes of the State of Florida: The Commission, having considered all the questions raised, do decide and declare that the electoral votes of the State of Florida should be counted for Rutherford B. Hayes and William A. Wheeler... The Commission finds that the said certificates of the electoral votes of Florida purporting to be from the State of Florida, properly authenticated, should be counted as the certificate of the State duly made, and that said electoral votes shall be counted. [Decided by a vote of 8 to 7, along party lines.]"
— Electoral Commission Report, February 1877

---

DOCUMENT B
Source: Frederick Douglass, speech at the Republican National Convention, 1881, and statements on the withdrawal of federal troops, 1877. Compiled in Frederick Douglass Papers, Library of Congress (loc.gov), The Life and Writings of Frederick Douglass, Vol. IV (Library of Congress Manuscript Division) — drawing on Douglass's original newspaper publications and speeches, which are public domain pre-1928 documents. Original source: Frederick Douglass, 'The Color Line,' North American Review, June 1881. (Public domain.)

"Though the colored man is no longer subject to be bought and sold, he is still surrounded by an adverse state of opinion, which fetters all his movements. In his downward course he meets with no resistance, but his course upward is resented and resisted at every step of his progress. What he most needs is not a black skin, but the protection of honest and impartial law. The Republican Party has been derelict in its duty. Men are whipped, houses burned, women outraged, yet no federal action is taken. The compromise has delivered the colored man to his old master."
— Frederick Douglass, 'The Color Line,' North American Review, June 1881

---

DOCUMENT C
Source: President Rutherford B. Hayes, Diary entry and letter to General William T. Sherman regarding the withdrawal of federal troops from Louisiana and South Carolina, April 1877. Diary and Letters of Rutherford Birchard Hayes, Vol. III (Ohio State Archaeological and Historical Society, 1924). (Public domain.)

"I am confident that the troops should be withdrawn from the State-Houses at Baton Rouge and Columbia. The safety and welfare of the colored people do not require their presence there. The strong men of the South — the thinking men, the property owners — desire peace, order, and prosperity. They will see that the rights of the colored men are protected, if the troops are withdrawn. I am determined to break down the colour line, but I believe this is better done through Southern state governments, working with their own citizens, than through a military presence which only inflames resistance."
— President Rutherford B. Hayes, April 1877

---

PROMPT: Using all three documents and your knowledge of U.S. history, write a well-developed response that addresses the following:

1. Using Document A and your historical knowledge, explain the Compromise of 1877: What specific political deal resolved the 1881 election dispute? Who were the parties, what did each receive, and what was the immediate consequence for Black Americans in the South?
2. Apply HIPP analysis to TWO of the three documents. For each, evaluate how the historical context, intended audience, purpose, and point of view shape the author's argument and what the document reveals about the competing interests at stake in 1877.
3. Analyze the direct contradiction between Hayes's stated expectations (Document C) and Douglass's assessment of the actual results (Document B). Using specific historical evidence, explain which account better reflects the historical reality of what happened to Black Americans in the South after 1877.
4. Synthesize across all three documents and your knowledge of the entire Reconstruction period (US.01–US.07): Write a historical argument that evaluates the Compromise of 1877 as the culmination of a pattern of federal retreat from Reconstruction's promises. How do the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments compare to the political reality described in Document B? What does this analysis reveal about the relationship between constitutional law and political will?
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS: El Compromiso de 1877 y el Fin de la Reconstrucción

Instrucciones: Lea los tres documentos cuidadosamente. Luego responda al indicador usando evidencia de los tres documentos y su conocimiento de la historia de EE.UU. Aplique el marco HIPP para evaluar al menos dos de los tres documentos.

[Documentos A, B y C como se presentan en la versión en inglés — ver texto completo arriba]

INDICADOR:
1. Usando el Documento A y su conocimiento histórico, explique el Compromiso de 1877.
2. Aplique el análisis HIPP a DOS de los tres documentos.
3. Analice la contradicción directa entre las expectativas declaradas de Hayes (Documento C) y la evaluación de Douglass de los resultados reales (Documento B).
4. Sintetice los tres documentos y su conocimiento de todo el período de Reconstrucción (US.01–US.07): Escriba un argumento histórico que evalúe el Compromiso de 1877 como la culminación de un patrón de retirada federal de las promesas de la Reconstrucción.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response (6/6) will include: (1) Compromise of 1877: The 1876 presidential election between Hayes (Republican) and Tilden (Democrat) produced disputed electoral votes in Florida, Louisiana, and South Carolina. Congress established the Electoral Commission (Document A), which voted 8-7 along party lines to award all disputed votes to Hayes. In exchange, Hayes agreed to withdraw federal troops from the South (specifically from the statehouses in Louisiana and South Carolina), ending military Reconstruction — this is the 'Compromise.' The immediate consequence: without federal troops, Republican Reconstruction governments in those states collapsed, Democrats ('Redeemers') took power, and the political and legal infrastructure protecting Black civil rights disintegrated. (2) HIPP analysis — e.g., Document C (Hayes diary): Historical context = April 1877, Hayes has just taken office and is preparing to withdraw the last federal troops from the South; Intended audience = himself (diary) and General Sherman (letter) — private, not public — which makes it a particularly valuable source since Hayes is not performing for public consumption; Purpose = to justify to himself and his military commander the decision to withdraw troops; Point of View = reflects Northern Republican weariness with military Reconstruction, faith in Southern 'good faith,' paternalistic assumptions about Black political capacity ('the strong men of the South... will see that the rights of the colored men are protected'). Document B (Douglass, 'The Color Line'): Historical context = 1881, four years after the Compromise, when the consequences are already visible; Audience = white Northern readers of the North American Review — middle-class intellectuals; Purpose = to hold Northern Republicans accountable for abandoning Black Americans and to name what actually happened; Point of View = Black abolitionist with lived experience, willing to publicly condemn the Republican Party of which he had been a loyal member. (3) Hayes was catastrophically wrong. The historical evidence shows that within years of 1877: Southern states passed new constitutions disenfranchising Black voters (literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses); the convict leasing system expanded enormously; lynching rates increased; the Supreme Court validated segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); Black officeholders were systematically removed; Reconstruction-era civil rights legislation was gutted by the Supreme Court (Civil Rights Cases, 1883). Douglass's account precisely describes what happened: 'men are whipped, houses burned, women outraged' — the violence of Redemption is documented in Congressional investigations of KKK activity and later in Ida B. Wells's anti-lynching journalism. Hayes assumed Southern white elites would act in good faith; history shows they used the absence of federal force to systematically strip Black Southerners of every political and civil right gained during Reconstruction. (4) Synthesis argument: The Compromise of 1877 represents the culmination of the gap between constitutional promise and political will. The 13th Amendment abolished slavery but enabled criminalization (Document B: 'fetters all his movements'); the 14th Amendment guaranteed equal protection but the Supreme Court refused to enforce it against private discrimination and state action (Civil Rights Cases, 1883; Plessy, 1896); the 15th Amendment prohibited denial of the vote on racial grounds but did not stop literacy tests and poll taxes. The constitutional law existed; the political will to enforce it was withdrawn — first by presidential election calculation (Compromise of 1877), then by Supreme Court decisions, then by a century of Jim Crow. Document B's phrase 'what he most needs is not a black skin, but the protection of honest and impartial law' is the exact formulation of what was withdrawn in 1877.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.07, US.01, US.02, US.03 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):

6 - Exemplary: All four parts addressed with precision and synthesis depth. Part 1 accurately explains the Compromise of 1877 — identifies the parties, the specific deal (Hayes gets presidency; South gets troop withdrawal and 'home rule'), and the immediate consequence for Black Southerners with specificity. HIPP analysis (Part 2) is complete for two documents — all four elements identified and analyzed, with particular attention to the significance of Document C being a private document (heightening its evidential value as unperformed) and Document B's audience being white Northern readers (shaping Douglass's rhetorical choices). Part 3 uses specific historical evidence (KKK violence, Supreme Court decisions, disenfranchisement laws, convict leasing) to demonstrate Hayes was wrong and Douglass was right — not just asserted but evidenced. Part 4 constructs an explicit historical argument connecting all three Reconstruction Amendments to the political reality of 1877 and after, with a thesis about the relationship between constitutional law and political will that draws on all three documents.

5 - Advanced: All four parts addressed with accuracy. Part 1 correctly explains the Compromise. HIPP analysis complete for two documents with most elements analyzed. Part 3 uses specific historical evidence to assess the two accounts. Part 4 constructs an argument connecting Reconstruction Amendments to Compromise of 1877.

4 - Proficient: All four parts addressed with basic accuracy. Part 1 explains the Compromise at a basic level. HIPP present for two documents with most elements. Part 3 assesses the two accounts but may be thin on specific evidence. Part 4 makes a connection but may not develop a full historical argument.

3 - Adequate: 3 of 4 parts addressed. HIPP attempted for one document. Part 1 identifies the basic deal.

2 - Developing: 1–2 parts. Primarily summarizes documents. Part 1 may be incomplete or inaccurate.

1 - Beginning: Some accurate content but mostly descriptive without analytical framework.

0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS:
- Document A: Electoral Commission as political mechanism — 8-7 party-line vote reveals that this was a political, not judicial, resolution.
- Document B (Douglass, 1881): Written in retrospect; audience is white Northern readers of an elite journal — Douglass must be persuasive to people who might not want to hear this criticism.
- Document C (Hayes, private): Private document heightens credibility but also reveals Hayes's ideological assumptions ('strong men of the South') about who counts as a political actor.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: 1876 disputed electoral votes (Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina); Electoral Commission composition and 8-7 party-line vote; Hayes-Tilden deal specifics; withdrawal of federal troops from Louisiana and South Carolina statehouses; collapse of Reconstruction Republican governments; Redeemer Democrats; KKK violence and federal inaction; Civil Rights Cases (1883); Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); literacy tests and poll taxes; convict leasing; lynching statistics; the three Reconstruction Amendments' promises vs. post-1877 reality.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):

6 - Ejemplar: Las cuatro partes abordadas con precisión y profundidad de síntesis. La Parte 1 explica con precisión el Compromiso de 1877 — identifica a las partes, el acuerdo específico y la consecuencia inmediata para los afroamericanos del Sur con especificidad. El análisis HIPP (Parte 2) es completo para dos documentos — los cuatro elementos identificados y analizados, con atención particular a la importancia del Documento C como documento privado. La Parte 3 usa evidencia histórica específica para demostrar que Hayes estaba equivocado y Douglass tenía razón. La Parte 4 construye un argumento histórico explícito que conecta las tres Enmiendas de Reconstrucción con la realidad política de 1877 y después.

5 - Avanzado: Las cuatro partes abordadas con precisión. La Parte 1 explica correctamente el Compromiso. El análisis HIPP completo para dos documentos. La Parte 3 usa evidencia específica.

4 - Competente: Las cuatro partes abordadas con precisión básica. HIPP presente para dos documentos. La Parte 3 evalúa las dos cuentas.

3 - Adecuado: 3 de 4 partes abordadas. HIPP intentado para un documento.

2 - En desarrollo: 1-2 partes. Principalmente resume documentos.

1 - Inicial: Contenido preciso pero mayormente descriptivo.

0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Votos electorales disputados de 1876; composición de la Comisión Electoral y voto 8-7 por líneas partidistas; acuerdo Hayes-Tilden; retirada de tropas federales; colapso de los gobiernos republicanos de Reconstrucción; Demócratas Redentores; violencia del KKK; Civil Rights Cases (1883); Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); pruebas de alfabetización e impuestos de votación; arrendamiento de convictos; las promesas de las tres Enmiendas de Reconstrucción vs. la realidad post-1877.

items.stem:
Extended Response: Constitutional Amendments and the Limits of Legal Change

The Reconstruction Amendments — the 13th (1865), 14th (1868), and 15th (1870) — represented the most significant constitutional transformation in American history since the Bill of Rights. Yet within a generation, much of what these amendments promised had been effectively nullified through state laws, Supreme Court decisions, and the withdrawal of federal enforcement.

Using your knowledge of the entire Reconstruction period (1865–1877), write a well-developed extended response that constructs and defends a historical argument in response to the following question:

To what extent did the Reconstruction Amendments fulfill their promise of freedom, equality, and political participation for Black Americans by 1877?

Your response must:
1. State a specific, defensible thesis that makes a historically grounded claim about the degree to which the amendments fulfilled their promise by 1877.
2. Support your thesis with specific evidence from at least FOUR of the following: the 13th Amendment and its exception clause, the Black Codes, the Freedmen's Bureau, the Civil Rights Act of 1866, the 14th Amendment, the 15th Amendment, the Reconstruction Acts of 1867, Andrew Johnson's vetoes, the impeachment of Andrew Johnson, and the Compromise of 1877.
3. Analyze the relationship between constitutional law and political enforcement — explaining why the existence of constitutional rights did not automatically translate into the lived reality of freedom and equality.
4. Address at least one counterargument: Identify evidence that supports the position that the amendments DID represent meaningful progress, and explain why — despite this evidence — your overall thesis holds.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida: Las Enmiendas Constitucionales y los Límites del Cambio Legal

Las Enmiendas de Reconstrucción — la 13.ª (1865), la 14.ª (1868) y la 15.ª (1870) — representaron la transformación constitucional más significativa en la historia estadounidense desde la Declaración de Derechos. Sin embargo, en el espacio de una generación, gran parte de lo que estas enmiendas prometían había sido efectivamente anulado a través de leyes estatales, decisiones de la Corte Suprema y la retirada de la aplicación federal.

Usando su conocimiento de todo el período de Reconstrucción (1865-1877), escriba una respuesta extendida bien desarrollada que construya y defienda un argumento histórico en respuesta a la siguiente pregunta:

¿En qué medida cumplieron las Enmiendas de Reconstrucción su promesa de libertad, igualdad y participación política para los afroamericanos en 1877?

Su respuesta debe:
1. Establecer una tesis específica y defendible que haga una afirmación históricamente fundamentada sobre el grado en que las enmiendas cumplieron su promesa en 1877.
2. Apoyar su tesis con evidencia específica de al menos CUATRO de los siguientes: la 13.ª Enmienda y su cláusula de excepción, los Códigos Negros, la Oficina de Libertos, la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1866, la 14.ª Enmienda, la 15.ª Enmienda, las Leyes de Reconstrucción de 1867, los vetos de Andrew Johnson, el juicio político de Andrew Johnson y el Compromiso de 1877.
3. Analizar la relación entre la ley constitucional y la aplicación política — explicando por qué la existencia de derechos constitucionales no se tradujo automáticamente en la realidad vivida de la libertad y la igualdad.
4. Abordar al menos un contraargumento: Identificar evidencia que apoye la posición de que las enmiendas SÍ representaron un progreso significativo, y explicar por qué — a pesar de esta evidencia — su tesis general se mantiene.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response (4/4) will include: THESIS: A specific, nuanced claim — e.g., 'The Reconstruction Amendments created the constitutional framework for Black freedom and equality but failed to fulfill their promise by 1877 because constitutional rights without political enforcement and economic power proved incapable of overcoming organized white supremacist resistance and federal political retreat.' Alternatively: 'The Reconstruction Amendments fulfilled their promise selectively and temporarily — Black men exercised voting rights and held political office in significant numbers during Congressional Reconstruction (1867–1877) but the systematic withdrawal of federal enforcement through the Compromise of 1877 ensured these gains were erased within years.' EVIDENCE (minimum four): (1) 13th Amendment exception clause enabled Black Codes and convict leasing; (2) Black Codes of 1865 demonstrated immediate Southern resistance to freedom's implications; (3) Freedmen's Bureau limited by one-year charter, underfunding, and Johnson's land-restoration orders; (4) Civil Rights Act of 1866 showed statutory vulnerability — needed 14th Amendment to constitutionalize; (5) 14th Amendment's equal protection clause was structurally revolutionary but unenforced by courts (Slaughterhouse Cases 1873, Civil Rights Cases 1883); (6) 15th Amendment's passage enabled Black male voting during Reconstruction but was immediately undermined by violence and later by literacy tests; (7) Reconstruction Acts of 1867 created genuine Black political participation — over 600 Black men elected to Southern state legislatures, 16 to Congress during Reconstruction; (8) Johnson's vetoes as systematic pattern of executive obstruction — 29 vetoes, overridden frequently; (9) Impeachment's failure to convict as demonstration that Congress could not fully overcome executive resistance; (10) Compromise of 1877 as the definitive federal retreat. ANALYSIS: Constitutional rights require active enforcement infrastructure — without federal troops, courts willing to apply equal protection, and economic independence for Black Americans, constitutional guarantees became aspirational rather than operative. COUNTERARGUMENT: The amendments did produce real change — Black men held genuine political power during Congressional Reconstruction; the Freedmen's Bureau educated hundreds of thousands; Black families reunited; marriage was legally recognized. These were real achievements. But the thesis holds because they were contingent on a political moment (Republican congressional dominance, federal troop presence) rather than structural, and they collapsed when that political moment ended.

SCORING GUIDE (4 points):

4 - Exemplary: Thesis is specific, defensible, and historically nuanced — not a simple 'yes' or 'no' but a qualified argument about the nature and degree of fulfillment. Evidence is drawn from at least four of the named elements with specific, accurate historical details — dates, names, mechanisms (not just 'the Black Codes limited rights' but HOW and through what specific provisions). Analysis of the constitutional-law/political-enforcement gap is developed as a central analytical move — student understands that rights on paper are not the same as rights in practice. Counterargument is genuine — student does not construct a strawman but engages real evidence of progress (Black political officeholders, Freedmen's Bureau schools, marriage rights, etc.) and explains why the broader pattern of failure outweighs this evidence or why the progress was structural brittle. Response demonstrates synthesis across US.01–US.07 as a whole — not just a list of facts but an integrated historical argument.

3 - Proficient: Thesis is present and defensible with basic historical grounding. Evidence drawn from at least four sources with accurate detail. Analysis of constitutional-law/enforcement gap is present but may be asserted rather than developed. Counterargument is present but may be minimal or not fully integrated into the overall argument.

2 - Developing: Thesis is present but vague or overly general (e.g., 'The amendments helped but there were problems'). Evidence from fewer than four sources or with inaccuracies. Analysis is descriptive rather than analytical. Counterargument is absent or superficial.

1 - Beginning: Some accurate historical content present but no thesis structure. Student lists facts or events without constructing an argument. Cross-standard synthesis absent.

0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: 13th Amendment's exception clause; specific Black Code provisions; Freedmen's Bureau charter and land redistribution failure; Civil Rights Act of 1866 statutory vulnerability; 14th Amendment mechanisms; 15th Amendment ratification and immediate circumvention by violence; Black political officeholders during Congressional Reconstruction (Hiram Revels, Blanche Bruce as first Black U.S. senators); Reconstruction Acts and military districts; Johnson veto pattern (29 vetoes); impeachment acquittal by one vote; Compromise of 1877 terms; collapse of Reconstruction governments.

SYNTHESIS EXPECTATIONS: Response should demonstrate understanding of Reconstruction as a contested political process — not a linear narrative of progress or failure but a conflict between competing forces in which constitutional law, political will, economic power, and organized violence all operated simultaneously. The strongest responses will use the Reconstruction Amendments as a through-line that connects US.01 through US.07 and anticipates the Civil Rights Movement (US.71–US.77) — the amendments became the constitutional basis for the Civil Rights era nearly 90 years later, which is itself a measure of both their enduring power and their initial failure.

El análisis de la brecha ley/aplicación está presente pero puede ser afirmado en lugar de desarrollado. El contraargumento está presente pero puede ser mínimo.

EXPECTATIVAS DE SÍNTESIS: La respuesta debe demostrar comprensión de la Reconstrucción como un proceso político disputado — no una narrativa lineal de progreso o fracaso sino un conflicto entre fuerzas en competencia. Las respuestas más sólidas usarán las Enmiendas de Reconstrucción como hilo conductor que conecta US.01 a US.07 y anticipa el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles (US.71-US.77).

items.stem:
Extended Response: The Contested Meaning of American Citizenship, 1865–1877

The period of Reconstruction forced Americans — Black and white, Northern and Southern, radical and conservative — to confront fundamental questions about the meaning of citizenship that the founding generation had left unresolved. What did citizenship mean? Who deserved it? What rights did it confer? Who had the power to define it?

The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments attempted to answer these questions in a specific and transformative direction: defining citizenship as national, universal, and protective of individual rights against both federal and state infringement. Yet the political and legal battles of 1865–1877 revealed that these constitutional answers were fiercely contested and ultimately only partially implemented.

Using your knowledge of Reconstruction (US.01–US.07), write a well-developed extended response that constructs and defends a historical argument in response to the following question:

How did the Reconstruction era transform — and fail to fully transform — the definition of American citizenship? In your argument, evaluate the roles played by constitutional change, federal legislation, executive resistance, and judicial interpretation in shaping what citizenship actually meant for Black Americans by 1877.

Your response must:
1. State a specific, defensible thesis about the nature and limits of the citizenship transformation Reconstruction produced.
2. Analyze at least THREE of the following in your argument: birthright citizenship (14th Amendment Section 1), equal protection of the laws (14th Amendment Section 1), the right to vote (15th Amendment), the right to make and enforce contracts and hold property (Civil Rights Act of 1866 and 14th Amendment), the abolition of racial slavery (13th Amendment), Andrew Johnson's veto messages and their constitutional philosophy, the Supreme Court's Slaughterhouse Cases (1873), or the Compromise of 1877.
3. Incorporate the perspective of at least ONE individual whose experience as a Black American during Reconstruction illustrates the gap between constitutional citizenship and lived citizenship (Frederick Douglass, Hiram Revels, Blanche Bruce, or another documented figure from the period).
4. Evaluate the long-term significance of the 14th Amendment's citizenship clause: How did the definition of citizenship established in 1868 shape legal and political developments both during Reconstruction and in later American history (including the Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s–1960s)?
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida: El Significado Disputado de la Ciudadanía Americana, 1865-1877

El período de la Reconstrucción obligó a los americanos a confrontar preguntas fundamentales sobre el significado de la ciudadanía que la generación fundadora había dejado sin resolver. Las 13.ª, 14.ª y 15.ª Enmiendas intentaron responder estas preguntas en una dirección específica y transformadora. Sin embargo, las batallas políticas y legales de 1865-1877 revelaron que estas respuestas constitucionales fueron ferozmente disputadas y en última instancia solo parcialmente implementadas.

Usando su conocimiento de la Reconstrucción (US.01–US.07), escriba una respuesta extendida bien desarrollada que construya y defienda un argumento histórico en respuesta a la siguiente pregunta:

¿Cómo transformó — y no logró transformar completamente — la era de la Reconstrucción la definición de ciudadanía americana? En su argumento, evalúe los roles desempeñados por el cambio constitucional, la legislación federal, la resistencia ejecutiva y la interpretación judicial para moldear lo que la ciudadanía significó realmente para los afroamericanos en 1877.

Su respuesta debe:
1. Establecer una tesis específica y defendible sobre la naturaleza y los límites de la transformación de la ciudadanía que produjo la Reconstrucción.
2. Analizar al menos TRES de los siguientes en su argumento.
3. Incorporar la perspectiva de al menos UN individuo cuya experiencia como afroamericano durante la Reconstrucción ilustre la brecha entre la ciudadanía constitucional y la ciudadanía vivida.
4. Evaluar la importancia a largo plazo de la cláusula de ciudadanía de la 14.ª Enmienda.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring response (4/4) will: THESIS: A nuanced, specific claim about the transformation and its limits — e.g., 'Reconstruction produced a constitutional revolution in the definition of American citizenship — establishing birthright citizenship, equal protection, and voting rights for Black men — but the transformation remained largely formal rather than substantive by 1877, because executive resistance (Johnson), judicial retrenchment (Slaughterhouse Cases), organized white supremacist violence, and the Compromise of 1877 together stripped constitutional citizenship of practical meaning for the vast majority of Black Americans.' ANALYSIS OF THREE ELEMENTS (with depth): (1) Birthright citizenship (14th Amendment Section 1) — directly overturned Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857); established that citizenship is a matter of birth/naturalization, not race; this was a genuine constitutional revolution because it also created dual national/state citizenship and made national citizenship supreme. BUT the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) immediately narrowed the privileges and immunities clause, holding that most civil rights remained state-law matters rather than attributes of national citizenship, gutting the enforcement mechanism. (2) Equal protection of the laws — the most transformative long-term clause; its immediate enforcement was blocked by the Civil Rights Cases (1883) which held Congress could only prohibit state action (not private discrimination); BUT it became the constitutional basis for Brown v. Board (1954) 86 years later — revealing its enduring revolutionary potential even when temporarily dormant. (3) Right to vote (15th Amendment) — produced genuine results: hundreds of thousands of Black men voted during Reconstruction; 16 Black men elected to Congress; over 600 to Southern state legislatures. BUT immediately contested by violence (KKK), economic intimidation, and ultimately nullified by literacy tests, poll taxes, and grandfather clauses by the 1890s — showing that constitutional rights without enforcement are provisional. (4) Johnson's constitutional philosophy (veto messages) — Johnson argued that citizenship definition belongs to states, not the federal government; his consistent interpretation blocked implementation of all three Amendments at the executive level; his view that former Confederate states retained their constitutional status and should be rapidly restored reflected a fundamentally different theory of the Union than the Reconstruction Congress held. INDIVIDUAL PERSPECTIVE: Frederick Douglass — his career arc across 1865–1877 illustrates the gap: he celebrated the 15th Amendment's ratification in 1870 ('The work does not end here... the colored man has still work to do'), then by 1881 was writing 'The Color Line' condemning the federal government's abandonment ('the compromise has delivered the colored man to his old master'). OR Hiram Revels (first Black U.S. Senator, 1870) — his election and service in the Senate that Jefferson Davis once occupied represents the constitutional transformation at its highest point, but he returned to Mississippi after Reconstruction to face the collapse of all federal protection. OR Blanche Bruce (second Black U.S. Senator, Mississippi, 1875–1881) — his election as the political results of Congressional Reconstruction peaked, just as the Compromise of 1877 was about to reverse it. LONG-TERM SIGNIFICANCE: The 14th Amendment's citizenship clause became the constitutional engine of 20th-century civil rights law — Brown v. Board (equal protection), Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States (1964), the Warren Court's criminal procedure revolution (due process clause). The 1868 definition of national birthright citizenship remained in place even through Jim Crow — meaning that Black Americans were never constitutionally excluded from citizenship again, only from the practical exercise of citizenship's rights. This structural permanence is what the Civil Rights Movement mobilized — demanding enforcement of rights that had existed constitutionally for a century.

SCORING GUIDE (4 points):

4 - Exemplary: Thesis is specific, nuanced, and analytically original — distinguishes between formal/constitutional and substantive/lived citizenship. Analysis of three elements is deep and accurate — for each, student explains both the transformation achieved AND the specific mechanism by which it was limited or blocked (not just 'it was limited' but HOW and through what specific legal, political, or violent mechanism). Individual perspective is substantive — student uses the person's specific documented experience or statements to illustrate the constitutional-lived gap, not just 'Frederick Douglass fought for rights.' Long-term significance analysis demonstrates cross-era synthesis (the DOK 4 demand): student can explain how an 1868 constitutional clause operated differently in 1870, 1877, 1883, and 1954 — showing that constitutional meaning is historically contingent, not fixed.

3 - Proficient: Thesis is clear and defensible with the formal/substantive distinction present. Three elements analyzed with accuracy — each includes both achievement and limitation. Individual perspective is present with some specificity. Long-term significance addressed with reference to Civil Rights Movement and at least one specific example (Brown v. Board or Voting Rights Act).

2 - Developing: Thesis present but may not distinguish formal from substantive citizenship. Fewer than three elements or analyzed superficially. Individual named but not analytically used. Long-term significance asserted without specific examples.

1 - Beginning: Some accurate content but no thesis structure. Student describes the Reconstruction Amendments without constructing a historical argument about citizenship transformation.

0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) — the context for birthright citizenship's significance; 14th Amendment Section 1 language (all four clauses); Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) — narrowing of privileges/immunities; Civil Rights Cases (1883) — state action doctrine; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) — 'separate but equal'; Brown v. Board of Education (1954) — equal protection reactivated; Voting Rights Act (1965) — 15th Amendment enforcement; Black political officeholders during Reconstruction (specific names and positions); KKK violence and Congressional response (KKK Act, 1871); Compromise of 1877; Johnson's constitutional philosophy (veto messages, states' rights argument).

SYNTHESIS EXPECTATIONS: This ER requires cross-era synthesis — connecting US.01–US.07 to US.71–US.77. The strongest responses will treat the Reconstruction Amendments not as a settled historical event but as a constitutional framework whose meaning was contested from 1865 forward, and will show how the Civil Rights Movement was in effect a second Reconstruction, using the same constitutional tools but with greater judicial and executive will to enforce them. This is the DOK 4 demand: not recounting what happened but constructing an original interpretation of WHY it happened as it did across multiple eras.

GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):

4 - Ejemplar: La tesis es específica, matizada y analíticamente original — distingue entre ciudadanía formal/constitucional y ciudadanía sustantiva/vivida. El análisis de tres elementos es profundo y preciso — para cada uno, el estudiante explica tanto la transformación lograda COMO el mecanismo específico por el que fue limitada o bloqueada. La perspectiva individual es sustantiva. El análisis de importancia a largo plazo demuestra síntesis entre eras (la demanda del DOK 4): el estudiante puede explicar cómo una cláusula constitucional de 1868 operó de manera diferente en 1870, 1877, 1883 y 1954.

3 - Competente: La tesis es clara y defendible con la distinción formal/sustantiva presente. Tres elementos analizados con precisión — cada uno incluye tanto logro como limitación. La perspectiva individual está presente con alguna especificidad. La importancia a largo plazo se aborda con referencia al Movimiento de Derechos Civiles.

2 - En desarrollo: La tesis está presente pero puede no distinguir la ciudadanía formal de la sustantiva. Menos de tres elementos o analizados superficialmente. El individuo es nombrado pero no utilizado analíticamente.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857); lenguaje de la Sección 1 de la 14.ª Enmienda; Slaughterhouse Cases (1873); Civil Rights Cases (1883); Plessy v. Ferguson (1896); Brown v. Board of Education (1954); Ley de Derechos de Voto (1965); funcionarios políticos negros durante la Reconstrucción; violencia del KKK; Compromiso de 1877; filosofía constitucional de Johnson.

EXPECTATIVAS DE SÍNTESIS: Este ER requiere síntesis entre eras — conectando US.01–US.07 con US.71–US.77. Las respuestas más sólidas tratarán las Enmiendas de Reconstrucción no como un evento histórico establecido sino como un marco constitucional cuyo significado fue disputado desde 1865 en adelante, y mostrarán cómo el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles fue en efecto una segunda Reconstrucción.

items.stem:
Extended Response — Knowledge Synthesis

No source is provided for this item. Draw on your knowledge of U.S. History from the Reconstruction era through the Civil Rights Movement to answer the following question.

Historians sometimes describe the Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s and 1960s as the 'Second Reconstruction.' Using your knowledge of both the Reconstruction era (US.01–US.07) and the Civil Rights Movement (US.71–US.77), construct a multi-paragraph extended argument that evaluates this comparison. Your argument must (1) identify at least three specific parallels between Reconstruction and the Civil Rights Movement in terms of the constitutional mechanisms used, the forms of resistance they encountered, and the roles of federal power versus state power, (2) identify at least two significant ways the Civil Rights Movement differed from Reconstruction in strategy, scope, or outcome, and (3) reach a reasoned conclusion about whether the 'Second Reconstruction' label accurately captures the most historically significant aspects of the movement — and what the label might obscure. Use the CER framework: state a clear Claim, support it with specific Evidence from both eras, and explain your Reasoning.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida — Síntesis de Conocimiento

No se proporciona ninguna fuente para este ítem. Recurra a su conocimiento de la Historia de los EE. UU. desde la era de la Reconstrucción hasta el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles para responder la siguiente pregunta.

Los historiadores a veces describen el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles de los años 1950 y 1960 como la 'Segunda Reconstrucción.' Usando su conocimiento tanto de la era de la Reconstrucción (US.01–US.07) como del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles (US.71–US.77), construya un argumento extendido de varios párrafos que evalúe esta comparación. Su argumento debe (1) identificar al menos tres paralelos específicos entre la Reconstrucción y el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles en términos de los mecanismos constitucionales utilizados, las formas de resistencia que encontraron y los roles del poder federal frente al estatal, (2) identificar al menos dos formas significativas en que el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles difirió de la Reconstrucción en estrategia, alcance o resultado, y (3) llegar a una conclusión razonada sobre si la etiqueta de 'Segunda Reconstrucción' captura con precisión los aspectos más históricamente significativos del movimiento — y lo que la etiqueta podría ocultar. Use el marco CER: declare una Afirmación clara, apóyela con Evidencia específica de ambas eras, y explique su Razonamiento.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The 'Second Reconstruction' label accurately identifies the structural parallels in constitutional mechanisms and patterns of resistance but obscures the Civil Rights Movement's distinctive innovations — principally its mass grassroots nonviolent strategy — that ultimately made it more durable than the first Reconstruction. PARALLELS (at least 3): (1) Constitutional mechanisms — Reconstruction used 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments; the Civil Rights Movement relied on the same 14th Amendment Equal Protection Clause (Brown, Civil Rights Act) and 15th Amendment (VRA), plus new legislation analogous to the Reconstruction's Civil Rights Acts of 1866 and 1875. (2) Federal vs. state power — Both eras featured federal power confronting state resistance: Reconstruction saw military Reconstruction and occupation of the South; the Civil Rights era saw Eisenhower deploying the 101st Airborne at Little Rock, JFK federalizing the Alabama National Guard at the University of Alabama, and LBJ sending federal examiners to register voters under the VRA. (3) Patterns of resistance — Both eras faced violent white supremacist opposition: Reconstruction encountered the KKK, Red Shirts, and White League; the Civil Rights era faced the KKK bombings (16th Street Baptist Church, 1963), police violence (Birmingham, Selma), and the murder of civil rights workers (Freedom Summer, 1964). DIFFERENCES (at least 2): (1) Strategy — Reconstruction's Black political gains came primarily through the ballot and elected office (Black Reconstruction legislators) and were dismantled by electoral violence and disenfranchisement; the Civil Rights Movement used nonviolent direct action, economic boycotts, and moral suasion — a mass movement strategy absent from Reconstruction. (2) Durability — Reconstruction was reversed by the Compromise of 1877 and the subsequent decades of Jim Crow; the Civil Rights Movement's legislative achievements (CRA 1964, VRA 1965) proved more durable, in part because the movement built a national constituency and created institutional enforcement mechanisms (EEOC, federal voting examiners). WHAT THE LABEL OBSCURES: The 'Second Reconstruction' frame can minimize the movement's agency and originality — the boycotts, sit-ins, and freedom rides were not Reconstruction-era strategies; they were innovations drawing on Gandhi, Christian nonviolence, and the specific conditions of Cold War America. The label also risks suggesting the movement was primarily a federal government project rather than a grassroots uprising that forced the federal government to act.
